bahrain.intro:
Bahrain is a small island kingdom in the Gulf, with old forts, traditional markets, modern malls and a food scene that mixes Gulf, Indian, Persian, Levantine and international cooking.

This page explains what Bahrain is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
Bahrain is known for its pearl diving history, the Bahrain International Circuit, which hosts Formula 1, and the Qal'at al-Bahrain fort, a World Heritage site. It is one of the more open and relaxed places in the Gulf, with a long tradition of trade.

Its small size makes it easy to move between old markets, beaches and modern districts in a day.

Machboos, a spiced rice dish with chicken, lamb or fish, is the national dish. Other local foods include muhammar, sweet rice served with fish, balaleet, a sweet vermicelli breakfast with eggs, and fresh grilled hammour fish. Halwa Bahrainiya, a gelatin like sweet scented with cardamom, is famous.

Karak tea, Arabic coffee and dates are offered to guests, and Indian and Pakistani restaurants are common because of the large expatriate community.

Manama has the souq, the Bahrain National Museum and the Al Fateh Mosque. The Bahrain Fort and the Tree of Life in the desert are popular, and Muharraq has a heritage trail linked to pearl merchants. Beach resorts are found in the west.

The Formula 1 race brings a lively season in spring.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Bab Al Bahrain gate and the souq beyond it, the Bahrain National Museum and the glass towers of the financial district. Adliya, with its galleries and cafes, is the creative quarter.

People gather in the evening for dinner, coffee and shisha along the waterfront.

Try machboos, grilled hammour, shawarma, falafel and Bahraini sweets. Arabic breakfast, with eggs, cheese, bread and tea, is a popular weekend meal. The city has a rich selection of Indian, Pakistani, Lebanese and Iranian restaurants, and many cafes serve karak tea.

Halwa Bahrainiya and dates make good gifts.

Visit the Bab Al Bahrain and the souq, the Al Fateh Grand Mosque and the National Museum. The Beit Al Quran has Islamic art, and Block 338 in Adliya has cafes and galleries. The Bahrain Bay area offers a modern waterfront.

The Bahrain Fort and Muharraq are nearby.

sections.h2: What Muharraq Governorate is known for
sections.body:
The governorate is known for the Pearling Path, a UNESCO listed trail of merchant houses, oyster beds and warehouses that tells the story of pearl diving. Muharraq keeps its old character in its narrow lanes, mosques and old coffee shops.

The area is also close to Arad Fort and to the Amwaj Islands.

Local food is traditional, with muhammar, machboos, grilled fish and balaleet at breakfast. Old coffee shops serve Arabic coffee, karak tea and traditional sweets. Seafood is fresh near the coast and small family restaurants dominate.

Halwa shops are a local landmark.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Muharraq Governorate
sections.body:
The Pearling Path, the Siyadi House, the Sheikh Isa bin Ali House and the Arad Fort are the key heritage stops. The Amwaj Islands have a marina, beach and restaurants, and the Bahrain Fort is close.

The airport makes this area convenient for stopovers.

It is also known for its football club, a strong local tradition.

Muharraq is the place for traditional Bahraini food. Try muhammar rice with fish, machboos, balaleet and fresh bread from local bakeries. Old coffee shops serve karak and Arabic coffee, and halwa shops sell sweets by weight.

Fish and seafood restaurants near the coast serve the catch of the day.

Walk the Pearling Path, visit the Siyadi House, the Bin Matar House and the Sheikh Ebrahim Center. The Bahrain Fort Museum is not far, and Arad Fort stands near the airport.

A guided walk helps explain the history.

Family run restaurants offer home style food.

Belgium is a small country with a big reputation for food. It is known for chocolate, beer, waffles, mussels and fries, and for medieval cities with grand squares.

sections.body:
Belgium is known for Brussels, the home of European institutions, for the medieval canals of Bruges and Ghent, and for Antwerp's diamonds and fashion. It has three official languages, Dutch, French and German, and each region has its own flavor.

The country has a strong cafe culture and a high standard of cooking, from simple brasseries to Michelin starred restaurants.

Frites with mayonnaise, served in paper cones, are a national obsession. Mussels with fries, waterzooi, a creamy stew, and stoemp, mashed vegetables, are traditional. Carbonnade flamande is a beef stew cooked with beer.

Belgian waffles, pralines and chocolate are world famous, and Belgium makes hundreds of beers, including Trappist ales.

The city is known for the Cathedral of Our Lady, with its tall spire, the Grote Markt, the Central Station and the diamond district. It is also home to the Rubens house and to famous fashion designers.

The city has a cosmopolitan feel, and its cafes and bars are lively late into the evening.

Try stoofvlees with fries, mussels, croquettes and Antwerp's famous hand shaped biscuits. Beer is a way of life, and brown cafes serve local brews. The city has a strong Jewish, Turkish and Moroccan food presence, and the harbor area adds fresh seafood.

Chocolate shops and bakeries are everywhere.

The Cathedral, the Grote Markt, the Rubens House and the Central Station are classic. The MAS museum offers a view, and the Zuid and Het Eilandje districts are good for walks. Mechelen and Ghent are short train rides away.

The Zoo, next to the station, is one of the oldest in Europe.

The region is known for the Grand Place, a spectacular square, the Atomium, the Manneken Pis and comic strip murals. It is home to many nationalities, which shows in its restaurants.

Brussels has art nouveau architecture, large parks and lively markets.

Waffles in two styles, light Brussels and sweet Liege, are sold in the streets. Fries, mussels, carbonnade and waterzooi are classic dishes, and chocolate shops line the central streets. Beer cafes serve lambic and gueuze, typical Brussels styles.

The city also has excellent African, Turkish, Italian and Asian food.

Visit the Grand Place, the Royal Palace, the Magritte Museum and the Atomium. The Sablon area has chocolatiers and antiques, and the Marolles flea market is a favorite.

The Parc du Cinquantenaire and the Forest of Soignes offer green space.

The city is known for the Grand Place, the Manneken Pis, the Atomium and its comic strip walls. Its art nouveau houses and museums add depth, and its markets are lively on weekends.

Brussels is a city of many languages and cultures, and its restaurants show this variety.

Brussels waffles, fries with mayonnaise, mussels in white wine and carbonnade are the classic tastes. Chocolate shops sell pralines and truffles, and beer cafes serve lambic, gueuze and abbey beers. Speculoos biscuits are a popular treat.

For a fuller meal, look for brasseries serving local dishes.

The Grand Place, the Royal Galleries of Saint Hubert, the Magritte Museum and the Atomium are major sights. The Comic Strip Center is fun for all ages, and the Cinquantenaire park is nice for a walk.

Bruges and Ghent are short train rides away.

Rain is common, so bring a jacket. Many restaurants close on Sunday. Tipping is optional because service is included.

The city is known for the Gravensteen castle, the three towers of the old town and the Ghent Altarpiece. The canals glow at night, and the center is largely traffic free.

Ghent is also known as a vegetarian friendly city, with many meat free options.

Waterzooi, a creamy stew of chicken or fish, is the signature dish. Try cuberdons, cone shaped raspberry candies, and mustard from Tierenteyn. Fries, mussels and stoofvlees are widely served, and the city has many vegetarian and vegan restaurants.

Brown cafes serve local beers, and bakeries sell fresh bread and pastries.

The Gravensteen, the Saint Bavo Cathedral, the Graslei and Korenlei quays and the Patershol district are the highlights. Boat tours on the canals give a different view, and the Citadelpark has museums.

Bruges and Brussels are easy day trips.

The canals and beguinage give the city a quiet, scenic side.

Try stoofvlees, mussels and local pastries.

The Town Hall, the University Library, the Grand Beguinage and the Vaartkom canal area are popular. The Botanic Garden and Arenberg Castle offer green space. Brussels is 20 minutes away by train.

The Oude Markt is the center of nightlife.

Liege waffles, with pearl sugar, are sold from street stalls. Boulets sauce lapin, meatballs in a sweet sour sauce, are a local classic, along with Herve cheese, Ardennes ham and sirop de Liege, a fruit syrup. Mineral water from Spa is famous.

The city is known for the Montagne de Bueren, a long staircase with views, the Guillemins railway station designed by a famous architect and the Sunday La Batte market along the river. Liege people are known for their friendliness and humor.

The city is also home to many festivals, including a famous Christmas market.

Liege waffles, with caramelized sugar, are the signature treat. Boulets, large meatballs in a sweet sour sauce, are usually served with fries. Herve cheese, Ardennes ham, sirop de Liege and local beers round out the table.

The La Batte market has food stalls and local products.

Climb the Montagne de Bueren, visit the Palace of the Prince Bishops and the Curtius Museum, and see the Guillemins station. Parc de la Boverie has an art museum and walks along the river.

Spa, Namur and the Ardennes are easy trips.

belgium/namur-province.intro:
Namur Province sits in the south of Belgium, with the Meuse river, castles, caves and hills.

This page explains what Namur Province is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What Namur Province is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for the city of Namur, its citadel, and the Meuse valley, which offers kayaking, cycling and scenic towns such as Dinant. The Ardennes forests and caves bring nature lovers.

The province is also known for its abbey beers and cheeses.

Dinant is known for couques, very hard biscuits, and flamiche, a cheese pie. Local dishes include game, Ardennes ham, trout and cheese. Abbey beers such as those from Maredsous and Rochefort are brewed in the region.

Chocolate, pralines and local jams are common gifts.

sections.h2: Places to visit in Namur Province
sections.body:
Namur has the Citadel and the old town. Dinant has a cathedral and cliff top citadel, and the Chateau de Freyr gardens and the Grottes de Han caves are popular. Kayaking on the Lesse river is a favorite summer activity.

The Maredsous abbey is a quiet stop.

belgium/namur-province/namur.intro:
Namur is the capital of Wallonia, set where the Sambre meets the Meuse, with a big citadel and a lively old town.

This page explains what Namur is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for its large Citadel, which offers views over the rivers and the city, and for its old town of pedestrian streets and squares. It is a student town with a relaxed feel.

The annual festivals and the Namur Folk Festival bring locals and visitors together.

Local cooking includes Ardennes ham, game, trout, cheese and the regional flamiche, a cheese tart. Beers from nearby abbeys are popular, and the town has bakeries and chocolatiers.

Brasseries serve moules frites, stoofvlees and waffles, and cafes have outdoor tables in summer.

The Citadel, the Cathedral of Saint Aubin and the Felicien Rops Museum are the highlights. The Place d'Armes and the pedestrian streets are good for cafes, and the Meuse riverfront offers walks.

Dinant and the Ardennes are close.

belgium/west-flanders.intro:
West Flanders is the coastal province of Belgium, with the canal city of Bruges, long beaches and poignant First World War sites.

This page explains what West Flanders is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.h2: What West Flanders is known for
sections.body:
The province is known for Bruges, a World Heritage city, for the Belgian coast with its long beaches and the Flanders Fields memorials around Ypres. Its villages and polders have a quiet beauty.

Beer, seafood and chocolate shape the local table.

The coast offers grey shrimp croquettes, fresh North Sea fish, mussels and fries. Bruges is known for chocolate, lace and beer, and the Westvleteren and other Trappist beers come from nearby abbeys. Waffles and pancakes are sold in every town.

Farm products and cheese are common in the countryside.

sections.h2: Places to visit in West Flanders
sections.body:
Bruges has the Markt, the Belfry, the canals and the Beguinage. Ostend has a long beach and a lively promenade, and Ypres has the Menin Gate and war museums. Kortrijk and Damme are nearby.

Cycling routes link the coast and the countryside.

belgium/west-flanders/bruges.intro:
Bruges is a well preserved medieval city of canals, cobbled lanes and old squares, and one of the most visited places in Belgium.

This page explains what Bruges is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for the Markt square with its Belfry tower, the Rozenhoedkaai canal view, the Beguinage and the Basilica of the Holy Blood. Boats glide along the canals, and horse drawn carriages cross the old center.

The city is also known for lace, chocolate and beer.

Try chocolate and pralines from many local shops, along with Belgian waffles, mussels and fries. Local dishes include stoofvlees, waterzooi and Bruges beer, such as the local Brugse Zot. Cafes serve hot chocolate and pastries.

The city has a growing selection of modern and vegetarian restaurants.

The Markt and the Belfry climb, a canal boat tour, the Church of Our Lady and the Beguinage are the highlights. The Minnewater lake is peaceful, and the windmills along the old ramparts are scenic.

A bike ride to Damme is popular.

Book ahead for dinner, especially on weekends and holidays.

Visit early or late to avoid crowds. Day trippers arrive by midday. The city is small and walkable. Rain is common.

belgium/west-flanders/ostend.intro:
Ostend is a seaside city on the Belgian coast, with a wide beach, a long promenade and fresh seafood.

This page explains what Ostend is known for, what to eat and where to go, and helps you use the listings to compare ratings, photos and locations before you choose a table.

sections.body:
The city is known for its beach, the old Kursaal casino building, its harbor and its art history, including the painter James Ensor. It is a popular weekend trip from Brussels and Ghent.

The city has an energetic summer season and a calm winter beauty.

Seafood is the main attraction, with fresh fish, mussels, grey shrimp and oysters. Fish soup and sole are local specialties, and ice cream and waffles are common on the promenade. Local beers pair well with fish.

The fish market and the harbor have stalls selling fresh catch.

The beach and promenade, the Ensor House, the Mercator sailing ship and the Fort Napoleon are popular. The coastal tram runs along the whole coast, making day trips easy.

Bruges is about 25 minutes away by train.

The coast can be windy. In summer, weekends are busy. Many seafood places close in winter on weekdays.
